title: Nuremberg: history and power
text:
Just watched the fabulous 2025 Netflix movie Nuremberg and the eerie resonance to the power dynamics in the world today!  The film follows U.S. Army psychiatrist Douglas Kelley, tasked with evaluating top Nazi leaders before trial—especially Hermann GÃ¶ring (number 2 man after Hitler).
It becomes a psychological duel: Kelley tries to understand how “ordinary” men commit extraordinary evil, while GÃ¶ring manipulates, denies, and reframes reality.
The courtroom drama shows a key turning point in history: choosing law over vengeance—trying war criminals publicly rather than executing them.
A central theme: evil is not always monstrous—it can be rational, charismatic, and self-justifying.
Ending message: even after justice, Kelley is haunted warning that such ideologies can re-emerge anywhere.

In one line:

It’s less about Nazis—and more about how humans justify violence, deny truth, and normalize brutality.

Humiliation of Germany after WW-1 lay the seeds for rearmament in Germany and a desire for retribution and restoration of former glory by a charismatic leader and a willing populace. Enactment of the "Nuremberg Laws" in 1935 preceded and justified the German military atrocities and imperialism.  

Seen against current tensions involving the United States, Israel, Iran, and the broader Middle East, the parallels are not about direct equivalence but about recurring human patterns of fear, hatred, divine permission, and a vision of greatness. All sides frame their actions as defensive or necessary, even as civilian harm and escalation become normalized. Narratives compete with reality, moral certainty hardens positions, and modern technology—drones, missiles, proxy warfare—creates distance from the human cost. As in Nuremberg, the deeper warning is that the mechanisms enabling large-scale violence—fear, nationalism, denial, and persuasive leadership—remain very much intact, while consistent systems of accountability lag behind power.

By the way, check out this excellent editorial by Ezra Klein in NYT: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/04/12/opinion/hasan-piker-democrats.html?unlocked_article_code=1.aVA.N863.QMyurFK9MuVy&smid=url-share

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/04/24/opinion/conspiracy-theory-tucker-antisemitism.html?unlocked_article_code=1.d1A.JDh2.Yw9Oq2V3Sg-w&smid=url-share

It clarifies the important distinction between antisemitism (really bad racism) vs. anti-Zionism (not so bad if you disagree with Israel's current military brutality). I look to Ezra Klein, Michelle Goldberg, and others to help me navigate these choppy waters!  I am deeply suspicious and skeptical about the American Right as to its talking points about Zionism (Tucker, Candice, Fuentes).
